newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Economists warn of fiscal risk in NZ budget.
newsitem.headline: Economists warn of fiscal risk in NZ budget.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters on Thursday proudly delivered his maiden budget, saying it contained sound economic management and compassionate social policy -- but economists said it also contained financial risk.
"Today, we set out our intentions for safe, prudent fiscal policy," Peters said.

But economists warned the government's commitment to a NZ$5 billion package of extra social spending over three years failed to build in the risk of any more deterioration in New Zealand's economic fundamentals.
"I think the concerning feature is the way there's been quite a significant shift in emphasis to the way fiscal risks are managed," said ANZ Bank chief economist Paul Stewart.

"Under previous administrations there was very strong commitment to running operating surpluses and repaying debt. The emphasis has now shifted much more towards spending, and there's much less emphasis on debt reduction," Stewart said.
"That's fine in its own right, but it means that there is significant risk that in the future the fiscal position will deteriorate further and will be back closer to balance or deficit."
Although Peters last week flagged a reduction in the 1997/98 surplus from the March projection of $3.3 billion, the budget's $1.5 billion forecast was below most analysts' estimates.

The substantial downward revisions of the operating surplus, Peters said, reflected in part the fact economic activity had not accelerated as quickly as the Treasury had earlier forecast, as well as a list of one-off factors.

The Treasury is now forecasting the surplus will rise to $1.9 billion in 1998/99 and to $2.6 billion in 1999/00, based on growth forecasts of 2.4 percent in 1998, 4.2 in 1999, and 3.5 percent in 2000.
"Though the surplus is reduced, it is still healthy and this confirms the wisdom of aiming for substantial surpluses to ensure continued debt reduction throughout the economic cycle," Peters said.
However, economists feared the budget's growth predictions were on the optimistic side and said even the sharply lower surpluses forecast faced the danger of shortfalls.

"If the economy does tend to be a bit flatter, as we think it will be, then that (1997/98) $1.5 billion surplus (forecast) might be revised down as we go through this year," said BNZ economist Peter Jolly.
"Certainly the near-term risk is on the downside."
While Peters conceded there was risk in the surplus forecasts, he said the budget signalled the government's intention to lift the momentum of pro-growth policies.
"There are always risks, but we have still got a solid buffer here in a $1.5 billion surplus. Only three countries in the world can make that claim," he told Reuters Financial Television.

"We, as a centre-right coalition, have delivered on sound economic management and we have delivered on compassionate social policy as well. That is unique in this country's political circumstances and I think we've got every reason to be proud of what we've done here today."
Opposition parties, however, slammed the budget, saying it provided no sense of direction.
Bancorp executive director Roger Kerr agreed, saying it contained "no great long-term economic strategising or planning of where New Zealand will be in five years' time." ($1 = NZ$1.46)
